intro.title: A guided tour
intro.body: This lab shows solved truco — for a handful of exact spots, the strategy no opponent can beat. This tour teaches you to read it, on one fixed spot: 11 × 11, a 4 turned up, so the 5s are the manilhas. Skip anytime; nothing here is graded.

spot.title: Set the stage
spot.body: The header sets the stage — the score and the turn-up. Nudge a score and the whole chart re-solves for the new stakes. Set it back to 11 × 11, then continue.

pickLead.title: You lead
pickLead.body: You are the leader. Play any card as your first move — a manilha, a throwaway, whatever you like. The rail records it and the responder answers next.

pickReply.title: The answer
pickReply.body: Now the responder plays. Pick any card to finish the opening exchange. From here the tour fixes one teaching line so the numbers hold still.

navArrows.title: Walk the hand
navArrows.body: Two cards are down. These arrows step back and forth through every decision in the hand — each one keeps its own chart.

navPlates.title: Jump to a decision
navPlates.body: Every decision is a plate. Click the Leader’s plate to jump straight there — the chart follows wherever you land.

editPast.title: Nothing is locked
editPast.body: Any past decision can be rewritten. Here the leader played a 3 — click 5♦ to change the line to the one we’ll study.

dealerActs.title: The dealer answers
dealerActs.body: With 5♦ led, it’s the dealer’s turn. This header frames the decision — who acts, which round, and the equity on the line — read it before the chart below.

stats.title: Reading the header
stats.body: The header keeps score: the leader’s <g>match equity</g> at this spot, and how <g2>often</g2> a deal even arrives here. Both are shares of the whole match, not this one hand.

badge.title: Blocks
badge.body: This brass L = 4 badge names the block — it fixes the leader’s shown card. Blocks carve the chart by what is already on the table; click the badge to switch blocks.

axes.title: The two axes
axes.body: Inside a block every cell is one hand. Rows are the H card, columns the M card — the two cards still in your hand. The arrows trace each axis.

cellPick.title: Pick up a hand
cellPick.body: Click the glowing cell — the hand 5♥ · 3 · 4, a manilha and two low cards. The panel on the right wakes up for exactly those three.

handAll.title: The hand panel
handAll.body: This panel is everything the solve knows about that hand: what each play is worth, how often you hold it, and how the plan shifts. We read it top to bottom.

handWin.title: What each play is worth
handWin.body: Each row prices one play — the dealer’s <g>match equity</g> if it acts now and both sides follow the solve, and what the play gives up beside it. These three sit far apart: that gap is real, not noise.

handOften.title: How often you are here
handOften.body: How <g>often</g> this exact hand arrives, and how much of the dealer’s range it is. Rare hands still count — this just says how much weight to give the lesson.

colors.title: Reading the colors
colors.body: The chart is colored by which card the solve plays: highest, middle, or lowest. A solid cell is one pure choice.

mix.title: When the solve mixes
mix.body: A split cell means the solve <g>mixes</g> — sometimes one card, sometimes another. These two are near 50/50: bluff-catch spots where always doing the same thing gets you exploited.

rangeMake.title: Make a range
rangeMake.body: Click the glowing card to blank it. The hand becomes a range — every card that could sit in that slot, all at once.

rangeVary.title: Read the range
rangeVary.body: That slot is now ?. Below, the range unrolls: one row per possible card, each showing how the solve plays that finished hand. Compare the manilha rows against the plain ones — same two known cards, different story. More on ranges in the guide.

pin.title: Pin it
pin.body: Pin the hand to carry it as you change the score or vira — the chart re-solves around it while everything else moves. Pin it now.

pinSee.title: Pinned hands travel
pinSee.body: Your pinned hand rides here on the rail and stays put as you explore other spots. Unpin whenever you like.

done.title: That is the tour
done.body: That is it. The ? button reopens this anytime, and every underlined term opens the guide in a new tab — Part I is the theory of the solve, Part II the player's handbook. Now go read some charts.

rules.title: The exact game the solver plays
rules.intro1: There are many trucos — and even “truco paulista” has no single standard. This page is the variant the solver actually plays, read straight out of the engine's code. Where the truco you grew up with differs, the engine wins: every chart in the lab is exact for these rules and no others.
rules.intro2: Two absences up front: no envido, no flor. The solved game is the three-round card fight plus the truco ladder — nothing else rides on it.
rules.cardsHead: The deck, the turn-up, the manilhas
rules.cardsP1: A 40-card deck: ranks 4 5 6 7 Q J K A 2 3 in the four suits — the 8s, 9s and 10s are out. Off the manilhas, that listing IS the order, weakest to strongest: 4 lowest, 3 highest, suits never matter, and two cards of the same rank tie.
rules.cardsP2: After dealing, one card is turned face up: the turn-up (vira). The rank right above it — wrapping 3 → 4 — becomes the manilha rank: those four cards outrank everything else, and only among them does the suit decide, strongest to weakest ♣ > ♥ > ♠ > ♦. So each manilha is one specific card: under a 4 turn-up, the 5♣ is the strongest card in the game.
rules.roundsP1: Three cards each, up to three rounds, one card per round; best of three wins the hand. The Leader — the Dealer's opponent — leads round 1; after that the round's winner leads, and a tied round keeps the same leader. Ties are where home rules diverge, so here is the engine's complete table:

tie1.def: has no winner; the hand continues and the same player leads again.

tie2.def: ends the hand at once for whoever holds the win — in either order, win-then-tie or tie-then-win. No third round is played.

tie3.def: the winner of the first non-tied round takes the hand — in a normal split, round 1's winner.

tie4.def: the hand goes to the Leader, the leader of round 1.

rules.fdP1: From round 2 on (never in round 1) a card may be played face down. Its identity is never revealed and never consulted: a face-down card loses to any face-up card, and two face-down cards tie. It is a pure sacrifice — a way to burn a card without showing your hand — not a hidden weapon.
rules.stakesP1: A hand starts at 1 point. Calling truco offers 3; the later raises climb one rung at a time up the ladder 1 → 3 → 6 → 9 → 12. A raise pauses the cards until it is answered: accept and play continues at the new value; decline and the raiser scores the previous value on the spot (decline the first truco and it's 1 point).
rules.stakesP2: Raises strictly alternate: whoever made the last raise cannot make the next one — only the opponent can escalate, whether by re-raising over a pending offer or by raising later in the hand. Conceding the hand is legal on any turn and pays the opponent exactly what a decline would — never less.
rules.elevenP1: When one player reaches 11 points, the next hand is a mão de onze: before any card is played, the player at 11 — and only them, even when the other seat would lead — chooses. Accept, and the hand is played for 3; fold, and the opponent collects 1. The truco ladder is locked for the whole hand, for both players.
rules.elevenP2: At 11 × 11 there is no decision to make: the hand is automatically worth 3, raises stay locked, and the cards are dealt and seen normally. The folklore “iron hand” — playing blind at 11 × 11 — is not part of this variant.
rules.matchP1: First to 12 points wins the match, and scores cap there — winning 3 at 11 lands exactly on 12. A hand ends the moment its outcome is fixed: if round 3 can no longer change the result, it isn't played out.
rules.aside: Solved truco is exactly this game. If a chart ever surprises you, check this page before doubting the math.

solving.title: What “solving” a game like truco even means
solving.p1: A solve is a pair of strategies — one per side — where neither can do better by changing, whatever the other does. Game theory calls it a Nash equilibrium. In a game of hidden cards and bluffing that can't be a single “best move”: it's a mix, tuned so the opponent can't read you. The whole idea fits in one tiny endgame you can solve by hand —
solving.toyHead: A bluff you can solve by hand
solving.toySetup: Final round, real stakes. Mão — the leader — has led a plain 3 — it's on the table, nothing left behind it. Pé, the dealer, arrives holding the top manilha (m♣, the 5♣ under v4) or a dead 4, equally often, and calls truco: the hand rises from 1 point to 3. Mão can fold — conceding the base point — or call and play the round out for 3. One deal, one bluff, one decision:
solving.toyP2: Should mão call? That depends on one number: p, the share of manilhas behind pé's truco. Calling collects 3 when the raise was air and loses 3 when the manilha shows; folding costs 1 for sure:
solving.toyFnote: Payoffs are points for mão, at the engine's real stakes: folding a truco concedes the previously accepted value (1); calling plays the raised hand (3). p is the probability the raise hides m♣.
solving.toyP3: At p* = 2/3 mão is exactly indifferent. A raising range richer than two-thirds manilha makes folding right; leaner, and calling prints. Everything the lab's charts show is this same arithmetic, repeated at scale.
solving.mixP1: Now hand the knob to pé. Raising the manilha is automatic — the choice is b, how often pé also raises the dead 4. Never bluff and every truco means the manilha: mão learns to fold, and pé's monster earns a single point. Always bluff and half the raises are air: mão calls every one and cashes 3 whenever the 4 turns up. Both pure habits are exploited the moment the opponent notices.
solving.mixP2: The equilibrium sits where nobody can be read. Pé bluffs just enough that the raising range lands exactly on mão's indifference point, and mão calls just enough that bluffing neither prints money nor burns it:
solving.mixFnote: b is pé's bluff frequency with the dead 4; c is mão's calling frequency. The 50/50 deal plus b* = ½ puts 2 manilhas behind every 3 raises — the p* above.
solving.mixTakeaway: A solved strategy randomizes on purpose — at exactly the rate that makes reading it worthless. Every mixed cell in the lab is doing this.
solving.cfrHead: How the machine solves the real thing
solving.cfrP1: The real game tree is far too large for hand arithmetic, so the solve is computed with counterfactual regret minimization: the program plays itself for billions of hands and, at every decision, leans a little more toward what it regretted not doing —
solving.cfrFnote: Rᵀ(a) tallies how much better always playing a would have done than the strategy actually played; positive regrets, renormalized, set the next mix — regret matching.
solving.cfrP2: Averaged over time, that self-play settles into the equilibrium, and the result is certified — checked action by action against a perfect best response — so “exact” means exact, within a stated tolerance.
solving.aside: Exact solving is expensive, and the lab bundles only selected chart exports. A grey Score or Turn-up choice means no chart for that exact spot is loaded here; it does not mean the spot is currently computing, or even that no solver artifact exists. The coverage ledger in the appendix — the numbers chapter — separates those cases.

chart.title: Reading a chart
chart.intro1: Each chart shows how the solve plays every possible holding at one decision. With all three cards unknown the lab never squeezes them into one flat grid: it draws exact blocks — one card pinned per block, the other two on the axes — so every cell is exactly one holding, never a family.
chart.intro2: The reader below turns up a 5 (v5), so the 6s are the manilhas: they beat everything, they carry their suit — 6♣ > 6♥ > 6♠ > 6♦ — and each is a single card, so a manilha row or column holds exactly one copy and appears alone. Plain ranks ignore suit entirely: a 3 is any 3.
chart.blocksP: Pin your weakest card to pick the block (this reader begins at L = 7), then run your highest card down the rows and your middle card across the columns. The brass label is itself the control — click it to change both the pinned slot and the one card this chart holds fixed. Hover or tap any cell —
chart.numberP: Only one number fits in a cell, so a mixed cell prints its biggest slice — the most-played action's percentage. The color bands carry the whole mix, each sized by its probability; the readout here (in the lab: the tooltip) spells out every action with its exact share.
chart.approxP: A cell wearing ≈ instead of a number is weak: where a per-node BR measurement ships, an adversarial best response gains more than 5 match-win points. Older exports use the legacy self-loss/reach alarm. Either way, read ≈ as a warning, not a tactic — the trust chapter shows the machinery.
chart.aside: the number = the biggest slice. the tooltip = the whole mix.
chart.listP: LIST lays the very same holdings out as rows, strongest first: the cards up front, the mix as a labeled bar. Nothing changes but the shape — the grid is for seeing regions at a glance, the list is for reading one hand at a time.
chart.listCaption: Real data — the first eight holdings of the same L = 4 block, exactly as the lab's LIST draws them; each bar segment is labeled with its action and share.
chart.walkHead: Walking one hand through the decisions
chart.walkP1: Pin the hand as it was actually played in the left rail, then walk the decisions with ← →. A chart cell fills two of your three cards; the panel’s card list or a card’s own menu fills the rest, and cells that are impossible with your picks grey out.
chart.walkP2: Pinning the hand (⚑) fixes it for the whole hand: that player’s rail decisions then show the pinned cards’ own mix, and only those cards stay playable. Click a card to clear it, double-click for its menu.
chart.walkAside: Think of it as replaying one deal in slow motion, asking at every fork: what does the solve do here?
chart.walkerCaption: Click a point in the rail: focus moves there, while the already observed cards stay in the line.

walker.dealP: Before a play, every hand is still possible. The chart describes that full starting distribution.
walker.leadP: The first open card is now history. It stays visible while you inspect the next player’s decision.
walker.replyP: This reply filters Pé’s range: hands that would rarely show it shrink in the next chart.
walker.nextP: The focus has moved, not rewritten the deal. Pin a hand to keep asking what that same hand does here.

ranges.title: Ranges — the hands still possible
ranges.intro: A range is not a vague feeling about what somebody might hold. It is the complete set of hands still possible at this decision, with a weight on each one. The line you watched filters that set: a hand that rarely chooses the observed actions becomes a small bar; an impossible hand disappears altogether.
ranges.toolHead: Build a range, then read it
ranges.toolP: Start with [? ? ?] for every legal three-card hand. Fix cards by typing their notation, clicking a slot and selecting a card, or dragging it onto a slot; all three inputs stay synchronized. GRID always draws every matching block. Its brass badge changes only the split — H, M, or L — while LIST gives the same arriving range as rows. Choose any holding to make it exact.
ranges.blockersP: A blocker is just a card that is already visible, so it cannot also be in a hand. The vira removes one copy before anybody acts; each open card in the line removes another. That is a physical deck constraint, not a solver preference. The lab greys choices with no copies left, and the range editor refuses them too.

blockerWidget.question: Chance Pé holds at least one 3
blockerWidget.takeaway: Click a card in Mão's hand to pin or clear it. The visible vira and every pinned card are removed from the deck before Pé's hidden hand is counted.
blockerWidget.caption: This percentage is conditioned on the cards visible at this table — not an abstract deck baseline. The vira picker deliberately excludes 2.

views.title: The four views
views.intro: Every cell in the lab answers one of four questions about the same solved decision: what does the solve do here (Strategy), which hands actually get here (Range), what would a fixed habit cost (Cost), and how does the play shift between two spots (Compare). The table gives all four at a glance; the sections below take them one at a time — formula first, then a figure of real solved cells drawn with the lab's own components.
views.tableHead: The four views at a glance

strategy.head: Strategy — the mix itself
strategy.shows: each action's share of the mix — the color bands; the printed number is the biggest slice
strategy.takeaway: When a cell mixes, so should you: a fixed habit in a mixing spot is exactly what a reader exploits.
strategy.p1: Fix one holding and the solve's answer is not a card but a probability for every legal action: σ(a | h), the average strategy at this decision. A cell draws that mix as color bands, each as wide as its action's share, and prints only the biggest slice as its number. The full mix is always one hover away — the tooltip and the hand panel spell out every action; the number alone never does.
strategy.fnote: The printed number is the modal share of the displayed mix. Every cell is one exact holding, so the bands are that hand's own σ — nothing is averaged.
strategy.note: Housekeeping, so tiny slices don't read as noise: an action displayed under 3% that also loses more than 1 pp of match equity is dropped and the rest renormalized. The export keeps the raw mix — the chart is just tidier than the raw decimals.
strategy.figCaption: Real data — 11x11 v4, mão's opening lead, the L = 4 block: every exact holding whose weakest card is a 4. 23 of these 87 cells mix; the number is the biggest slice, and the ≈ treatment would mark any under-trained cell (this block has none).

range.head: Range — who actually arrives
range.shows: each holding's share of the acting player's arriving range; shading tracks the heaviest cell
range.takeaway: Ranges are earned, not dealt — every action a player survives filters what they can still be holding.
range.p1: A range is every hand a player could still hold at a decision, each weighted by how often it is actually held here. That weight is Bayes' arithmetic: start from how often the deal produces the holding, then multiply in σ for every observed action along the line. The chart normalizes those weights into shares of the arriving range.
range.p2: This is why ranges move as you walk. Each decision multiplies in another σ, and holdings that would rarely have played the observed line quietly drain out of the picture — fold-happy hands vanish after an accept, weak hands vanish after a confident lead. The toy tree in the solving chapter is the smallest case: one truco from pé instantly reweights his range to two-thirds manilha.
range.fnote: The export ships w(h) precomputed per node — the lab only normalizes and shades.
range.figCaption: Real data — 11x11 v4 : 4 6 — pé answered mão's 4 with a 6 and now leads round 2. Each cell is one exact pair of remaining cards; the % is its share of pé's arriving range, shaded against the heaviest cell. The weights carry σ(reply 6 | h): holdings that would rather have answered differently sit pale.

cost.head: Cost — the price of a habit
cost.shows: how much the priced habit gives up against the best available action, per holding
cost.takeaway: Dark cells are where discipline pays; pale cells forgive almost any habit.
cost.p1: Cost prices mistakes instead of describing the mix. For each holding it lines up what the available actions are worth — v(a) — and charges the gap between the best action and the one your habit takes. WORST ACTION prices the biggest blunder on offer; MOST-PLAYED prices the milder habit of always taking the solve's most-played action instead of mixing.
cost.p2: Two currencies: hand points — the 1 · 3 · 6 · 9 · 12 at stake this hand — or match-win percentage points, where the solver's equity q (±1) converts at 50 pp per unit: win % = 50 + 50 q.
cost.figCaption: Real data — the same block as the Strategy figure (11x11 v4, opening lead, L = 4), priced with WORST ACTION in match-win pp, IGNORE HIDES on. '·' cells are cost-flat: any card does. The dark cells are the holdings where a lazy habit actually bleeds — compare them with their mixes above.

compare.head: Compare — same decision, another spot
compare.shows: how far the same decision drifts between two solved spots — accept gap at bids, total variation elsewhere
compare.takeaway: If Compare lights up, the score changed the play — don't carry one chart across scoreboards.
compare.p1: Compare loads the same decision from a second solved spot and colors the disagreement. At bid decisions — the mão de onze, a pending raise — each cell shows the signed accept gap: green where the other spot accepts more, red where it folds more. At card decisions it shows total-variation distance: the share of play that would have to move to turn one mix into the other, from 0 (identical) to 100 (opposite).
compare.fnote: σ′ is the other spot's mix. The cell picks Δaccept exactly when the decision offers accept / fold; otherwise TV.
compare.figCaption: Real data — the opening lead after the accept, mão at 10 (11x10 v4) versus mão at 2 (11x2 v4), block L = 4. Gold marks holdings the trailing mão plays differently. At the mão-de-onze accept itself this comparison is nearly blank — between these scores the accept threshold barely moves.

views.selIntro: The toolbar's selectors don't change the machinery — they change which question Cost answers, and which actions count.

points.desc: prices COST in hand points — the 1 · 3 · 6 · 9 · 12 at stake this hand — instead of match equity. Good for feel; equity stays the real yardstick, since the same points matter differently at different scores.

ignoreHides.desc: keeps face-down plays out of Cost's best/worst pool whenever an open play exists, so the number prices which card you pick rather than whether you hide it. Toggle it off to price the hiding decision itself. The mix's most-played action can still be a hide — only the pool is filtered.

mostPlayed.desc: the default COST baseline: what you give up by always taking the single most-played action instead of the true mix.

worstAction.desc: the adversarial baseline: what the most expensive available action gives up — the size of the worst mistake on offer at each cell.

views.headIntro: Two numbers ride above every chart, and both come from the same weights as Range.

equity.desc: the acting player's match-win chance from this decision if both sides follow the solve — the range's reach-weighted average of each holding's mix value, mapped to a percentage.

reach.desc: how often a match in this band walks exactly this line — the node's total weight over the band root's. Low-reach corners earn little training, which is where the ≈ flag lives (see the trust chapter).

abstractions.title: The lossless abstractions behind the solve
abstractions.intro1: The solver does not keep two names when the rules can never tell them apart. It renames strategically identical cards, copies, and seats, solves that shared game once, then restores the familiar names in the lab.
abstractions.intro2: This is not hand bucketing and not an estimate. Every reduction on this page is a lossless isomorphism: it preserves every legal action, chance, payoff, and continuation. The tree is smaller; the game is unchanged.
abstractions.suitsP1: Outside the four manilhas, suit never affects strength or legality. A plain 3 of diamonds and a plain 3 of clubs therefore have the same future against every possible hand. The solver keeps one plain-3 class; the lab can print any of its four physical suits when needed.
abstractions.suitsAria: The four suited plain threes map to one plain-three class
abstractions.copiesP1: Once plain suits are irrelevant, physical 7s are interchangeable. What matters is only how many remain. In the example below one 7 is already visible, so the tree stores one rank with three remaining copies instead of three named cards. Every newly visible 7 subtracts another copy.
abstractions.copiesAria: After one seven is visible, the three remaining physical sevens map to one class with three copies
abstractions.rolesHead: Three public facts select one subgame
abstractions.rolesP1: The match is not solved as one monolithic tree. At every new hand, three public facts select a bounded subgame: the score, the dealer assignment, and the turn-up card. Each changes the game that follows, for a different reason.
abstractions.factorsAria: A score, dealer assignment, and turn-up card combine to select one exact hand subgame
abstractions.factorScoreWhy: Sets mão de onze, the legal raise ladder, and the value of every score reached next.
abstractions.factorDealerWhy: Determines mão and pé: who leads now, whose score sits in each role, and who deals next.
abstractions.factorTurnupWhy: Fixes card strength, the reduced deck class, and the probabilities of abstract deals.
abstractions.rolesP2: The solver then rewrites the first two facts in role order. Seat 0 and seat 1 are service identifiers; mão leads round one and pé dealt the hand. Dealer assignment is therefore not discarded and not an extra ×2: it decides which physical player's score occupies each role slot. Rotate the dealer without changing either player's points and the ordered score swaps.
abstractions.rolesAria: With seat zero on five and seat one on seven, changing the dealer changes the role-ordered score and selects a different subgame
abstractions.roleExampleNote: Same physical score in both cases: seat 0 has 5 · seat 1 has 7. The dealer assignment changes which ordered subgame is solved.
abstractions.backsolveP1: Here is the real dependency. At 10 × 11, the player on 11 faces the mão-de-onze choice: accept and play the hand for 3, or fold and concede 1. Accepting makes this hand match-deciding either way. Folding instead creates the next hand at 11 × 11, with the dealer rotated. So the correct fold value is whatever the already-solved 11 × 11 game is worth to this player — not simply “minus one point.”
abstractions.backsolveP2: The solver therefore solves both dealer orientations of 11 × 11 first, across the nine turn-up classes, and stores their chance-weighted continuation values. It substitutes the appropriate stored value into the fold leaf of every 10 × 11 tree, then solves the accept-or-fold decision. Repeating that substitution moves the solution backward through the match. The current turn-up affects the accept branch; after a fold, the deck is reshuffled and the next turn-up is sampled afresh. This is exact dynamic programming, not a truncated horizon.
abstractions.censusHead: How many subgames does that create?
abstractions.subgamesP1: That normalization gives the grid immediately. Mão and pé can each have 0 through 11 points, so dealer-oriented score produces 12 × 12 = 144 role-ordered states. The deck has ten concrete turn-up ranks but only nine exact structural classes; the next section proves the one merge, vira 2 ≡ vira 3. Dealer is not another ×2 because it has already decided which physical score belongs to pé.
abstractions.censusAria: Twelve mão scores times twelve pé scores times nine turn-up classes equals one thousand two hundred ninety-six exact subgames
abstractions.subgamesP2: Together these are 1,296 exact one-hand subgames. This is what the lab's Score, Dealer, and Turn-up controls select: the score and dealer choose the role-ordered state, and the turn-up chooses one of its nine card trees. They are coordinates of a policy, not cosmetic labels.
abstractions.viraHead: Two turn-ups can be one exact class
abstractions.viraP1: The surprising case is vira 2 ≡ vira 3. With vira 2, the 3s become manilhas and only three plain 2s remain. With vira 3, the 4s become manilhas and only three plain 3s remain. Rename every strength one step around the deck and the structures match exactly: eight full plain ranks, one three-copy top plain rank, and four suit-ordered manilhas.
abstractions.viraP2: That is why the picker may show either 2 or 3 while loading the same exact solution. Your chosen or typed rank is still remembered in every concrete card label; only the strategically identical structure is shared.
abstractions.exactNote: Nothing is averaged together here. If two deals would ever permit a different action or payoff, they cannot share this class.

visual.caption: Read either row straight across: eight full plain ranks, one three-copy top plain rank, then four suit-specific manilhas. The concrete names shift, but the inventory and every strategic relation stay fixed — so the two rows share one exact solution.

dependencies.aria: A score dependency tree showing how solved future scores unlock earlier role-ordered scores
dependencies.treeAria: Solve eleven by eleven first; it unlocks eleven by ten and ten by eleven, which then unlock the earlier score lattice down through nine by nine
dependencies.kicker: Backward induction · one score layer at a time
dependencies.title: Solved futures unlock earlier scores
dependencies.edge: arrow: solved continuation → newly solvable score
dependencies.hoverHint: Hover or focus a score to inspect its stored match equity.

A node with two incoming arrows — such as 10 × 10 or 9 × 9 — waits for both continuations. The dotted branches continue backward beyond this slice.

abstractions.simTakeaway: How much do the coordinates matter? It has been measured, over converged neighboring solutions: neighboring turn-up classes are nearly interchangeable wherever play actually goes, while neighboring scores disagree on about a seventh of actual play, concentrated in the hand's first moves. That asymmetry is why solutions transfer across turn-ups far more cheaply than across scores.
abstractions.sizesTakeaway: How large those trees get — and how much of the 1,296-subgame grid is solved so far, at what cost — is ledger material, kept with the rest of the measurements.

notation.title: Writing a spot down
notation.p1: Everything the lab shows fits on one line — the HAND field. Score, turn-up, a drafted hand, the walked history: the line and the lab stay in step both ways, and it lives in the page URL, so a spot you write down is a spot you can share, bookmark, or paste back later.
notation.p2: Try the two checks below. The lab checks the same grammar as you type and says exactly what it couldn’t read; omitted sections simply keep their current state.
notation.grammarP: Read the line as a small sentence: name the score and turn-up, optionally draft either role’s cards, then put the played history after :. Square brackets always hold three cards, strongest first.
notation.historiesP: A history is written in the order actions happen. / marks a completed round, * hides a card, and a accepts a raise or the hand of eleven when one is pending.
notation.quizP: These are deliberately small. They use the same parser as the HAND field, so a correct answer is a line the lab can understand.

grammar.caption: The notation is a language for describing one exact study state. Brackets and the colon make its boundaries easy to scan.

spot.desc: The score, turn-up, drafts, and history are optional sections of one state. A bare colon clears only the history.

draft.desc: Use mao for the leader and pe for the dealer. ! keeps that hand pinned while you walk the line.

card.desc: Plain ranks need no suit. A manilha must name its suit, or use md / ms / mh / mc. ? (or .) leaves a slot unknown.

history.desc: Actions run left to right. / is optional, but when written it must follow the second card of a completed round.

action.desc: A card can end in * to play face down. r starts truco; later rungs are r6, r9, and r12. a and f answer a pending decision.

examples.fixedText: At 10–10 with turn-up 4, the dealer is pinned to 5♦, 3, and one unknown card. The first round ends after 3 and J; then truco is called and accepted.
examples.elevenText: At 11–8 the leader must first accept or fold; this line writes the explicit accept. It then shows a 5♦ lead, a completed round, and a face-down 3.

options.wrongRole: The dealer’s pinned hand is 5♦, 3, and one unknown card.
options.wrongKnown: The leader’s fixed hand is 5♦, 3, and 2.

quiz.readCorrect: Exactly: mao names the leader, ! pins it, and ? is still an unknown slot.
quiz.readAgain: Read the role before the bracket, then the !, then each of the three slots.
quiz.writePrompt: Write a pinned leader hand containing 5♦, 3, and one unknown slot. Spacing is optional.
quiz.writeCorrect: The parser accepts it. That is a valid pinned range draft.
quiz.writeAgain: Not quite. Include mao, !, three bracketed slots, 5d, 3, and ? — in that strength order.

trust.title: How far to trust it
trust.intro: A solution is not a promise that every printed mix is equally polished. The lab now measures the important question at a node: how much can a perfectly adapting opponent gain from the strategy shown here? The answer is the quality badge; the older reach and self-loss numbers explain why a corner went bad.
trust.badgeHead: The quality badge is the headline
trust.badgeP: The badge is a per-node adversarial best-response gap, expressed in match-win percentage points. It compares the exported mix with a genuine opponent best response, rather than asking the solve to grade itself.
trust.solidDef: The measured exploit is at most one match-win point. Read the mix normally.
trust.cautionDef: There is visible room for an opponent to gain. Use it as a clue, not a prescription.
trust.weakDef: The lab replaces the strategy number with ≈. This branch is not reliable strategy.
trust.badgeAside: A BR table is shipped with the solved spot when this measurement is available. Older exports keep the legacy warning as a compatibility fallback.
trust.warningP: This is an actual 11×10 pilot continuation from the lab. The pale ≈ cells are not merely low probability: each has a measured best-response gap above 5 pp. Hover or tap a cell to see its own measurement.
trust.warningCaption: Real lab data — 11×10 v4, after the mão de onze is accepted and a low-reach first-round continuation. {n} of the exact two-card grid’s 87 cells are weak by their measured BR gap, so the lab renders ≈ instead of a strategy number.
trust.warningTakeaway: Don’t infer a tactic from an ≈ cell. Step back to the last solid decision, or explore a different line.
trust.diagnosticsHead: Why an off-path mix gets noisy
trust.diagnosticsP: Before the BR table, the lab's warning came from two diagnostics. They stay here because they explain how a corner went bad — they describe training coverage, not quality.
trust.selfLossQ: the solve’s equilibrium value after action a at holding h
trust.selfLossScale: converts the solver’s −1…1 value scale into match-win percentage points
trust.selfLossNote: Self-loss asks whether the mix is close to its own best action under the solve's q values — an alarm, not an adversarial guarantee.
trust.ownLine: the acting player’s earlier decisions on the line
trust.ownReach: how often that player’s own exported strategy walks this holding to the node
trust.ownReachNote: Near-zero own reach means the averaging almost never collected experience here; the legacy alarm uses ε = 0.001.
trust.pruningP: The cause is concrete: once a non-owner action's probability reaches zero, CFR stops descending into that branch — correct for a truly dominated action, but it freezes whatever early random values sit below. Low own reach records that history; the BR gap says whether the result is actually exploitable.
trust.certificateHead: What the certificate does — and doesn’t — say
trust.certificateP: The solve’s certificate is a whole-game, reach-weighted bound against exact best responses. It says the strategy profile is close to equilibrium on average across the deal tree. A tiny off-path branch contributes almost nothing to that average, so the certificate alone cannot certify every cell. That is why the per-node BR measurement belongs on the chart.
trust.certificateTakeaway: Trust the node’s own badge first. Use the global certificate to understand the solve as a whole, and self-loss plus own reach to understand how a warning arose.

eleven.title: The hand of eleven, charted
eleven.lede: Part II begins where the theory pays off fastest: the one decision every player on eleven must make, hand after hand, with nothing hidden and no future streets to fear. These are the solve's own accept/fold charts, digested for the table.
eleven.stakesP1: At eleven points the next hand changes shape: the side on eleven looks at its three cards and answers — fold, conceding one point, or accept, playing the hand for three. The decision belongs to the side on eleven whoever dealt, and raises are off the table for the rest of the hand.
eleven.stakesP2: That makes it the cleanest question in truco: one look, yes or no. It is also the decision the solve prices most exactly — every chart in this chapter is a certified equilibrium read straight off the solved spots.
eleven.stakesAside: Both sides on eleven is a different animal: the 11×11 hand is played out for the match — automatically worth three, with no accept/fold step at all — so it does not appear below.
eleven.readingP1: The grids are the same ones Part I taught: each mini-chart fixes the lowest card — the L badge — and its axes place the other two. Blue accepts, vermillion folds. Unlike most nodes, the answer here is almost never mixed: of the 403 distinct hands, at most a handful mix at any score. The frontier is a line you can memorize.
eleven.readingP2: Hover or tap a cell and the readout prices both answers: match-win chance if you accept, match-win chance if you fold, and the gap between them in percentage points. Folding is worth the same whatever you hold — its value is the score, not the hand.
eleven.chartsP1: Pick the opponent's score. At 11×10 it matters whether the side on eleven deals the hand or leads it, so that score appears twice.
eleven.plateSummary: The solve accepts {accept}% of dealt hands here · folding wins {fold}% of matches.
eleven.plateHint: Hover or tap a cell — the readout prices accepting and folding that exact hand.
eleven.plateClose: A genuine coin-flip — either answer costs almost nothing.
eleven.plateFoldCosts: Folding this hand gives up {pp} pp of match-win chance.
eleven.plateAcceptCosts: Accepting this hand costs {pp} pp of match-win chance.
eleven.plateCaption: Every solved eleven decision, rendered from the same certified exports as the lab.
eleven.shapeP1: From 11×0 through 11×8 the range barely moves: the solve accepts roughly 60% of dealt hands at every one of those scores. What changes is the price of sloppiness. At 11×0 even the worst possible error costs about 2 pp — folding everything still wins you 97.6% of matches from there. By 11×8 the same bad habits cost up to 31 pp.
eleven.shapeP2: 11×9 is the tight corner. A lost accept hands the match away — nine plus three is twelve — while folding still leaves a comfortable 63.4%. So the range snaps shut: only 44% of hands accept, the tightest chart on this page, and calling with the very worst holding (4 · 4 · 4) is the dearest single mistake anywhere in the chapter, 63 pp of match-win chance.
eleven.shapeP3: 11×10 splits on the deal. Folding sends the match to 11×11, and that hand's value swings on who deals it. When the side on eleven is dealing here, the fold is under water — 44.7% — so the solve gambles, accepting 62% of hands. Leading instead, it can fold its way to 55.3% and tightens to 37%.
eleven.shapeAside: Three manilhas are never a fold — walking them away at 11×10 burns 55 pp. The expensive habits all live at 11×9 and 11×10; those two charts are the ones worth memorizing first.

leads.title: Opening leads
leads.lede: Every hand of truco starts the same way: the leader looks at three cards and puts one on the table. This chapter is that decision, read straight off the solved roots — which card opens, when the strongest card waits, and what the wrong choice costs in match-win chance.
leads.questionP1: The leader's options at the root are wider than they look: play any of the three cards face up — or, when the raise ladder is live, call truco before playing anything. The solve almost never takes that last road: at 10×10 the immediate truco carries just 0.3% of its opening mix. Leverage is worth more after a round has been seen.
leads.questionP2: What the solve weighs in choosing the card is everything the theory chapters built: which round the hand most wants to win, what the lead reveals about the two cards behind it, and — at live-ladder scores — which continuations keep the truco threat pointed the right way.
leads.chartsP1: The grids are Part I's own: each block fixes the lowest card, the axes place the other two, and a cell's colours are the solve's actual mix over first actions — dark blue leads the strongest card, sky the middle, vermillion the lowest, purple calls truco first. Hover or tap a cell and the readout prices every available opening for that exact hand.
leads.plateSummary: Leads the strongest card on {top}% of deals · the middle card {mid}% · the lowest {low}% · calls truco first {raise}%.
leads.plateHint: Hover or tap a cell — the readout prices every opening for that hand.
leads.plateVerdict: Percentages are the solve's mix; win % is the match-win chance after that opening, and −pp marks what the inferior openings give up.
leads.plateCaption: The leader's first decision at the solved roots, rendered from the same certified exports as the lab.
leads.patternsP1: At 10×10 the headline is simple: lead strength. The strongest card opens on 58% of deals, the middle on 22%, the lowest on 19%. But the rule has a load-bearing exception — the manilha stays home. Hands holding at least one manilha are 28% of deals, and they open with the manilha only 12% of the time; when the strongest card is a manilha, the solve banks it and leads something else at 83%. “Lead strength” really means: lead your best plain card, keep the certain round in your pocket.
leads.patternsP2: The locked stakes flip the policy. At 11×11, with the hand automatically worth three and no ladder left to threaten, the same 403 hands lead the lowest card 45% and the middle 39% — the strongest card opens just 17% of deals. With nothing to leverage, the opening becomes a probe: spend the cheap card, learn the round, and keep the winners for the rounds that decide the match.
leads.patternsP3: Two more measured facts worth keeping. The lead decision is mostly crisp — 233 of the 403 charted hands at 10×10, and over 330 at 11×11, commit to one opening outright; the rest genuinely mix. And at 11×11 it barely matters who deals: the two roles' lead policies agree to within a tenth of a percentage point.
leads.patternsAside: The two spots differ in exactly one structural fact — whether the truco ladder is still alive. That one difference is worth a 40-point swing in how often strength opens the hand.
leads.pricesP1: Averaged over deals, picking the worst available first card costs about 5 pp of match-win chance at 10×10 — and about 11 pp at 11×11, where there is no later ladder to claw a bad opening back.
leads.pricesP2: The expensive traps cluster where the hand is strongest: holding the club manilha with two middling cards, the worst opening burns close to 20 pp at 10×10, and the same family reaches 44 pp at 11×11. Strong hands don't make the opening safe — they raise the stakes of getting it wrong. Walk any of these cells in the plate above and the readout shows exactly which openings bleed.

raising.title: When to raise, when to let go
raising.lede: The truco is the game's one lever of pure pressure — and the decision players argue about most. This chapter reads the lever off the solved 10×10 spot from both sides: when the equilibrium actually pulls it, what its raising range is made of, and how it answers when the pressure comes back the other way.
raising.ladderP1: One structural fact frames everything at this score: the first truco already plays for the match. Ten plus three clears twelve, so once truco is accepted there is nothing left for six, nine, or twelve to add — the solver proves the higher rungs irrelevant here and removes them. Every raising question at 10×10 is the question of the single truco.
raising.ladderP2: And the solve is in no hurry to ask it. Calling truco before playing anything carries 0.3% of the opening mix — leverage is worth more once a round has been seen. The ladder is a mid-hand weapon, not an opening one.
raising.timingP1: Deal-weighted over the solved window, here is how often a truco actually gets called at each moment of the hand (only counting spots where no raise has happened yet):
raising.timingReply: Facing the lead, before replying (the dealer)
raising.timingTied: Leading round 2 after a tied round 1
raising.timingDeep: Round 2, after its first card is down
raising.timingP2: Two patterns stand out. A tied first round is truco weather — the rate jumps from 5% to 32%, because a tie converts round 2 into sudden death and the pressure play prices best exactly there. And the rate climbs as the hand ages: information arrived, ranges narrowed, and the threat has more to lean on.
raising.timingAside: Holding a manilha roughly doubles the urge: at the round-2 lead, manilha hands raise 12.5% against 5.1% for plain hands.
raising.rangeP1: Add up everything that raises across the window and look inside the range: 51.8% of the raising mass holds a manilha, against a 28% base rate. In other words, the solve's trucos are roughly half value, half pressure — enough strength that the call is honest, enough air that folding everything to it is exploitable.
raising.rangeP2: That mixture is the practical lesson. A truco from the equilibrium is not an announcement of the best hand; it is a priced threat that happens to be backed by one about half the time. Both pure readings — “truco means manilha” and “truco means bluff” — lose to it.
raising.answerHead: When to let a hand go
raising.answerP1: The answering side is where the money is. Facing a truco, the solve folds 63% and accepts 37% of its reach mass (re-raising is moot here — the higher rungs are score-irrelevant). Folding a majority of the time is not timidity; at these stakes conceding one point is routinely cheaper than playing three behind.
raising.answerP2: The habits are priced in the leaks chapter, but the headline belongs here: accepting every truco costs 10.4 pp of match-win chance per deal on average, and the single worst call in the window — accepting on 4 4 4 after leading a 4 into the raise — burns 36.6 pp. The mirror habit, folding everything, costs 6.2 pp: expensive, but the cheaper of the two sins.
raising.answerAside: All prices here are one-shot deviation prices: what the habit loses against the equilibrium opponent at that node, in match-win percentage points. Deeper trucos — round 3, and every line past the export window — are walked live in the lab.

leaks.title: The habits that cost the most
leaks.lede: Every player carries rules of thumb. This chapter prices six of the most common ones against the solve — not as insults but as a bill: the average cost per deal of following the habit where it applies, and the single worst hand it ruins. The expensive habits are not the ones folklore warns about.
leaks.pricingP1: Each price is a one-shot deviation: at every node where the habit prescribes an action, we charge the gap between that action's certified match-win value and the best available action's, weighted by how often the deal arrives there. The unit is percentage points of match-win chance per deal — the same pp the lab's COST view and the eleven chapter use.
leaks.pricingAside: One-shot means the opponent stays at equilibrium and your future self returns to it. A habit's long-run cost against an adapting opponent is higher — these are floor prices.
leaks.habitAcceptEleven: Accept every mão de onze at 11×9
leaks.habitFoldEleven: Fold every mão de onze at 11×10, dealing
leaks.habitLeadManilha: Open with the manilha when you hold one (10×10)
leaks.habitLeadStrongest: Always open with your strongest card (10×10)
leaks.tableP1: The ordering is the finding. The dear habits are answering habits — how you respond to a truco or a mão de onze — and the cheap ones are leading habits. Always opening with your strongest card, the folk rule most often repeated, costs barely a point per deal; calling every truco costs eight times as much, and auto-accepting the eleven at 11×9 costs twenty times as much.
leaks.readingP1: The two eleven rows point opposite ways on purpose: at 11×9 the range snaps shut and the leak is accepting too much, while at 11×10 dealing the fold is under water (44.7%) and the leak is folding too much. The same instinct — “be careful at eleven” — is a virtue at one score and a 19 pp tax at the other. Score first, then cards.
leaks.readingP2: The lead habits are cheap for a structural reason the opening-leads chapter charts: most hands have several openings within a point of each other, so even a dogmatic rule usually lands near the frontier. The traps are concentrated — the zap-led hands at ~20 pp — rather than spread. Answering decisions have no such cushion: accept and fold diverge by whole hands, not fractions.
leaks.readingAside: Prices measured off the certified 10×10 and 11×N tc0 exports (2026-07-18); the worst-hand column names the export window's dearest single row. Where a habit spans scores, its price moves with the score — check the lab before generalizing.

numbers.title: The solutions, by the numbers
numbers.lede: Part I explains what the solve is; this appendix is its ledger. Every statistic the project has measured about the shipped solutions — how big the game is, how much of it is solved, how tightly each spot is certified, how alike neighboring solutions are, how crisp optimal play is, and what it took to compute — collected on one page. Each figure is a dated entry in the project's benchmark log.
numbers.censusP1: One subgame per (score, dealer assignment, turn-up class): 1,296 in all, each spanning 140,118 distinct deals once the lossless equivalences collapse the raw card combinatorics. Within a subgame the tree grows with how much of the raise ladder is still alive.
numbers.censusP2: Those are the raw trees. The production tree also removes provably irrelevant branches — score-aware raise pruning plus proof-scoped prunes — cutting the deepest tier from 6.70B to 3.80B nodes (756.8M information sets) with no change in exactness. The shipped charts live in the two smallest tiers: an eleven root is a 49.6M-node tree, and a truco-band spot like 10×10 is a ~200M-node tree over 39.5M information sets.
numbers.censusAside: A node is one state of the game tree; an information set is one decision as a player actually faces it — own cards and the public line, not the opponent's cards. Charts draw one row per information set.
numbers.certHead: What ships, and how it's certified
numbers.certP1: The current Study release carries 225 solved spots — the per-(score, turn-up, dealer) artifacts of the coverage above. Each spot ships with an exact self-certification: a genuine best response is computed against the exported strategy from both seats, and the average of the two gains is the spot's exploitability ε, on the scale where ε 0.01 ≈ 0.5 percentage points of match-win chance. By how the spot was produced:
numbers.certTransferred: Transferred from a neighbor, then warm-refined
numbers.certP2: Transfers had to clear hard gates — raw ε ≤ 0.01, purified ε ≤ 0.004, weighted mean per-node best-response gap ≤ 0.25 pp — or the worker discarded the candidate and solved the spot natively. Native solves converge much tighter globally (median ε 0.00001), but 28 of them carry broader per-node profiles — which is exactly what the lab's per-cell ≈ badges exist to surface.
numbers.certAside: Purified ε is measured after near-zero mixture tails are snapped to the best action for export — it usually tightens the bound. The per-node column is the reach-weighted mean of the same per-cell best-response gaps behind the trust chapter's badges.
numbers.simP1: Solve two neighboring subgames independently to convergence and compare them row by row. Two averages tell different stories: over all table rows, and weighted by how often play actually reaches each row. TV is total-variation distance — the share of probability mass that would have to move to turn one row's mix into the other's (0 = identical).
numbers.simP2: The asymmetry is the finding. Changing the turn-up class barely moves play anywhere: on-path distance stays near 0.02 and the root decision shifts by 0.005. Changing the score concentrates its whole effect exactly where play goes — the root accept/fold row moves by 0.196, depths 1–3 by 0.12–0.18, and only about half of play mass sits on effectively identical rows. A small, shallow, score-sensitive core carries roughly half of the played game.
numbers.simAside: Wherever both neighbors are confidently pure (top action above 0.99 on both sides), they pick the same action in 99.99–100% of rows. The crisp part of optimal play is stable across neighboring subgames.
numbers.purityP1: Call a row pure when its biggest action takes more than 99% of the mix. Mixing dominates the tables — but not the played game:
numbers.purityP2: Half-plus of actual play sits at (near-)pure decisions — the same rows that agree at 99.99%+ across neighboring solutions. The complement is just as real: roughly 45% of play mass is genuinely mixed, the part of optimal truco that resists crisp human rules. Tighten “pure” to 99.9% and on-path purity drops to 50.7% (11×10) and 39.3% (10×10) — crispness softens with the cutoff.
numbers.effortP1: The solver is synchronous CFR+, adopted after measuring a ~10× cut in iteration count at the same certified ε. The 225-spot release was built by four preemptible cloud workers in 3–4.5 hours each — transferring a neighbor's solution wherever the certificate allowed (85% of spots) and re-solving natively where it didn't — for on the order of $5 of compute. A truco-band warm solve now peaks at ~16 GiB and ~18 minutes; a chain of memory work brought the same job down from a 75-GiB machine class.
numbers.effortP2: Certifying is cheap next to solving: one exact whole-game best response of the deepest tier — the full raise ladder from 0×0, 14.6 billion node visits — fits in 8.1 GiB and under three hours. The frontier is the deep solve itself: merely building the 0×0 tree in memory needs over 150 GiB, which is why the lattice below the shipped bands is approached bottom-up, subgame by subgame.
numbers.effortAside: Sources: the project benchmark log's dated entries, 2026-07-15 → 2026-07-17 — tree censuses, compare-policies, policy-stats, the 225-profile release fleet, and the deep-band scouts.
numbers.censusPruneP: Except during mão de onze, the engine still permits the ordinary raise ladder. The solver removes a higher re-raise only once lower score + current stake ≥ 12: at that point the current hand already decides the match for either winner, so escalating adds no prize and no rational fold leverage. This is value-exact pruning, not a claim that those buttons are illegal. The diagonal endpoints are compact anchors: 0 × 0 → 2 × 2 also covers unequal scores such as 2 × 10 and the mirrored 10 × 2. The table shows what the solver keeps with vira 4, for one dealer orientation, across every abstract deal.
numbers.treeNote: Exact vira-4 counts; other turn-up classes have not all been counted at every tier.
numbers.coverageAria: Two hundred sixteen of one thousand two hundred ninety-six exact tabular subgames are solved as of July 2026
numbers.coverageRemaining: 1,080 subgames remain outside the exact tabular solution
numbers.coverageP1: Exact strategies exist for 216 of 1,296 subgames: all 23 role-ordered score states where mão or pé is on 11, across all nine turn-up classes (207), plus 10 × 10 across all nine classes (9). The other 1,080 have not been solved as a full tabular grid.
numbers.coverageP2: The release behind that coverage stores 225 artifacts — one per (score, turn-up, dealer seat): every 11 × N score in both dealer orientations, plus 10 × 10 in one. The two counts differ by exactly the symmetric 11 × 11, whose two orientations are the same game with the seats renamed — nine artifacts covering nine subgames counted once. The Study Lab itself bundles a 15-chart subset of the release, all with vira 4.
numbers.coverageNote: The remaining grid is parked, not quietly computing. The measured census estimates about $505K spot / $1.12M on-demand to finish it tabularly, with a full-ladder job needing roughly 1.54 TB of RAM. The current direction uses exact subgames as teacher data, then extends coverage with a distilled neural policy and self-play; those later stages are not solved or certified yet.

score.desc: leader × dealer, up to 11 each — here both sides sit at 10.

vira.desc: v4: the turn-up’s rank is 4, so the 5s are the manilhas.

role.desc: pe[…] drafts the dealer’s cards; mao[…], the leader’s. A ! pins the hand for the whole walk.

hand.desc: exactly three slots, strongest first: 5d is the 5♦ manilha, 3 a plain three, ? a slot left unknown.

colon.desc: everything after : is the played history, action by action.

play.desc: a bare rank: off the manilhas, suits don’t matter, so 3 is any three.

play2.desc: pé answers with a jack. Two cards down — that completes the round.

round.desc: / asserts a round ended right there. Optional — the lab writes it for readability and checks it lands on a real boundary.

raise.desc: r calls truco. The later rungs are r6, r9, r12.

answer.desc: a accepts a pending raise (or the hand of eleven); f folds it.

mao.def: the deal’s leader — acts first in round 1. Also simply “the hand”: the deal being played.

pe.def: the dealer’s seat — answers last in round 1.

vira.def: the card turned face up after dealing; the rank right above it becomes the manilha rank.

manilha.def: the four cards one rank above the turn-up — the strongest in play, ordered ♣ > ♥ > ♠ > ♦.

zap.def: table slang for the club manilha — the strongest card in the game. The English chapters say “the club manilha”; at the table you will hear zap.

ladder.def: the raise ladder 1 → 3 → 6 → 9 → 12. Truco is the first rung; each later raise climbs one rung, and raises strictly alternate between the players.

eleven.term: hand of eleven · mão de onze
eleven.def: the hand dealt when one player stands on 11: that player looks at their cards and either accepts (the hand plays for 3) or folds (conceding 1). The ladder is locked either way.

iron.def: folklore name, and an ambiguous one: traditionally the 11 × 11 hand played blind, but often used for 11 × 11 generally. In this variant the 11 × 11 hand is played with open cards, automatically worth 3 — the guide just says “11 × 11”.

spot.def: one exact hand game selected by score, dealer, and turn-up — the coordinates the lab's controls set. The solver solves the match one spot at a time, from the finish backward.

solve.def: a certified equilibrium: a pair of strategies neither side can improve against, computed by self-play and checked against exact best responses.

equity.def: your chance of winning the match from here, if both sides follow the solve.

pp.def: one hundredth of match-win chance, the guide's price unit. The solver's q scale (±1) converts at 50 pp per unit: win % = 50 + 50q.

range.def: every hand a player could hold at a spot, each weighted by how often it actually arrives there.

blocker.def: a card that is visible — the turn-up, or any open play — and therefore cannot be in a hidden hand. A deck fact, not a solver preference; blockers are what strike hands from a range.

reach.def: how often a line of play actually happens under the solve — low-reach corners get little training and deserve less trust.

pure.def: a spot where the solve always takes the same action — a single-colour cell.

mix.def: a spot where the solve deliberately randomizes to stay unreadable — a multi-colour cell. The printed number is the biggest slice; the tooltip holds the whole mix.

selfloss.def: a weak per-node quality measurement: the lab shows ≈ when an adversarial best response can gain more than 5 match-win points. Self-loss and own reach explain the warning; they are not its headline test.

eps.def: how much a perfect best response gains against a strategy, averaged over both seats — the number a spot's certificate bounds. ε 0.01 ≈ 0.5 pp of match-win chance.
